h1: Brewing a saison at home when the weather is hot
title: Brewing a Saison at Home in Hot Weather | Craft Beer School
desc: Why saison is the beer to brew in an Indian summer: a recipe, how warm to ferment, stalled fermentations, diastaticus yeast and bottling safely.
teaser: Most beers suffer in the heat. Saison yeast likes it. Here is how to brew one when your kitchen is at 32 °C.
standfirst: Most homebrewers in India spend summer fighting heat with ice and wet towels. Saison takes the opposite approach. Its yeast was chosen for warm farmhouse fermentation, so the heat that ruins a pale ale can work for you.
sections:
Saison comes from the farmhouses of Wallonia in southern Belgium. The story usually told is that it was brewed in the cooler months and kept for farm workers in summer. What survives today is a pale, very dry, highly carbonated ale of roughly 5% to 7% ABV, with fruity, peppery and spicy yeast character. Our saison guide covers the style's history and range.

The traditional saison yeasts are unusual. Many ferment cleanly and well at temperatures that would make other ale yeasts produce solvent and hot alcohol flavours. Some strains are happiest in the high 20s °C and tolerate low 30s. That makes saison one of the few styles you can brew in an Indian summer without elaborate cooling.

For 20 litres at an original gravity of about 1.052:

  • Pilsner malt: 3.8 kg (82%)
  • Wheat malt: 0.45 kg (10%)
  • Munich malt: 0.15 kg (3%)
  • Plain white sugar: 0.25 kg (5%), added in the boil
  • Hops: about 25 to 30 IBU from Saaz, Styrian Goldings or East Kent Goldings, with a small late addition
  • Yeast: a saison strain, liquid or dry

Mash low, around 63 to 64 °C, for 75 to 90 minutes. You want a highly fermentable wort. The sugar helps dry the beer further. A saison should finish around 1.002 to 1.006, giving a crisp, almost champagne like dryness.

Warm does not mean uncontrolled. Pitch around 20 to 22 °C and let the temperature rise freely over the first few days as the yeast heats the beer. Many saison strains do their best work in the mid to high 20s °C. A free rise to 28 or 30 °C is common practice. Starting cool and rising gives a cleaner, more complex beer than pitching straight into 32 °C wort.

In practice, in a hot Indian kitchen you may not need to do anything. Pitch in the early morning when the room is coolest, then let the day's heat take over. If you live somewhere that sees 40 °C, a simple water bath keeps the beer from going past the yeast's comfort zone. Our guide to fermenting through an Indian summer covers easy ways to take the edge off.

One of the best known traditional saison strains is notorious for fermenting fast and then stalling around 1.030 to 1.035 for days or weeks. Nobody agrees fully on why. Some brewers point to temperature, others to pressure from a sealed fermenter. The usual advice is to keep the beer warm, around 30 °C, rather than letting it cool when fermentation slows. Give it time. Rousing the yeast by gently swirling the fermenter can help. Some brewers also loosen the lid so the beer is not under any back pressure.

Several popular dry saison yeasts do not stall at all. They belong to a variety known as diastaticus, which can break down sugars that normal brewing yeast leaves behind. That is why they finish so dry. It also means they can keep fermenting in the bottle. Make sure fermentation has fully finished, with the same gravity three days apart. Clean and sanitise your kit thoroughly afterwards. Keep separate tubing and plastic parts for these yeasts if you can. Diastaticus in a later batch of pale ale is how bottles over carbonate months after brewing.

Saison is traditionally very lively, around 2.8 to 3.5 volumes of CO2. Standard thin beer bottles may not be safe at the top end. Use heavy bottles designed for higher pressure, or aim for about 2.7 to 2.8 volumes in ordinary crown cap bottles. Our guide to carbonation levels by style explains the numbers. Store the bottles in a closed box while they condition.

A good saison is pale gold to light orange, with a big rocky white head. It smells of pepper, citrus and orchard fruit. It tastes dry, lightly bitter and refreshing, with no solvent burn and no lingering sweetness. It pairs well with spicy food, from Goan sausage to Andhra pickles.

Because the yeast leads, small changes in temperature and timing change the beer a great deal. Learning to steer that is what Belgian brewing is about.
faqs: How hot can I ferment a saison?
Many saison strains work well in the mid to high 20s °C and tolerate low 30s. Pitch a little cooler, around 20 to 22 °C, then let it rise.
Why has my saison stopped at 1.030?
Some traditional strains are known for stalling. Keep the beer warm, around 30 °C, rouse the yeast gently and give it time rather than bottling.
Only if it gets into other beers or into bottles before fermentation is complete. Clean thoroughly and wait for a stable gravity before bottling.
Can I use regular beer bottles for saison?
Yes for moderate carbonation around 2.7 to 2.8 volumes. For the very high levels some saisons reach, use heavy bottles rated for pressure.
